title: Pogo's Ripple Path
markdown:
Willow Creek Pond held the sky like a tray, all shimmer and gold. On that bright water, Pogo the pond skater danced. His legs were long and thin, threads spun from moonlight, and they barely dimpled the surface as he glided. He had a habit, a special dance that made the water giggle in tiny perfect circles. Round he spun, legs pushing just so, leaving rings of silver that widened and faded like smiles on the pond’s face.

Nell the newt watched from the roots of the old willow that dipped its branches in, moss-green eyes, small even for a newt. She was a watcher. Her mind buzzed with questions as quiet and steady as a bee in clover. Why those circles, so neat, so exact? They did not seem to go anywhere special. They just appeared. Were they for chasing sunbeams? A secret message for the fish? She whispered the puzzle to a passing water strider, who was always in a hurry and rippled past, leaving Nell her thoughts. Pogo, lost in his watery ballet, never noticed the little green observer tucked behind a broad lily pad.

The pond smelled of sun-baked earth, sweet clover, and damp. Reeds clicked. A frog visited and left. Dragonflies stitched the air. Nell stayed. Looking was her work.

One afternoon a breeze, playful and baked-earth soft, lifted a duck feather — white, cloud-light — and set it sailing. The little boat did not drift into the slow dark reeds. It headed for open sun.

Nell’s heart gave a hopeful tick. The feather boat seemed so small, so alone on the vast gleam. The breeze was warm on her skin. Water whispered past her hiding place, a dizzy swirl of light and shadow. Then, as if the pond had spoken his name, Pogo began to skate. Graceful as ever — and something new. The circles were no longer only pretty patterns. They were leading. They made a shimmering silvery ribbon, a secret invitation. Nell held her breath. The feather, as if guided by a current of kindness, began to follow.

Pattern had become path.

His legs blurred. Cool bright water swirled. The ribbon steered the little boat away from a patch of slow tangled weeds, the kind that snag tiny hulls and hold them fast. The path curved and swirled, a silent talk between skater, pond-skin, and feather. Sunbeams danced on the ripples until they sparkled like a trail of tiny diamonds. Slowly, with quiet confidence, the boat rode each ring as if it were a step. Pogo widened the circles, making the safe passage clearer still.

Nell did not move. She only looked, which was her way of helping. A calm hush sat on the pond, as if the water too were holding its breath.

A last graceful swirl delivered the feather to a small sun-drenched bank, to rest between two smooth grey pebbles: a perfect tiny boat on a perfect tiny shore, ready for whatever the wind decided next.

Pogo did not take a bow. He drew a new circle, perhaps for a minnow, perhaps for the joy of the line. Nell’s shade under the willow felt warmer, as if a sunbeam had found a gap in the leaves. The pond held the sky again. The pebbles kept the feather. The next ring opened, and opened, and faded, exactly as before, and not quite.
